Volodymyr-Volynsky Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Volynska oblast, Ukraine

Demolished. Volodymyr-Volynsky — known in Yiddish as Ludmir — holds one of the most significant rabbinic legacies documented in this collection: its Jewish community, first recorded in 1171, was led by renowned rabbis including Itzhak ben Bezalel (1542–1576) and the legendary Yom Tov Lipmann Heller (1634–1643), a towering halakhic authority, with Volyn represented in the Council of Four Lands by the community's own rabbis. In 1792, Moshe Gotlib founded a Hasidic dynasty in the town, and Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin, founder of the Karliner Hasidic dynasty, was also among its most prominent figures. In the 19th century, Hannah Rochel Verbermacher — known as the Maiden of Ludmir — lived here and drew a large following as a preacher, becoming the only known female tzadik in Hasidic history. By the second half of the 19th century, the town supported seven synagogues and a Jewish hospital, reaching 20 synagogues by the 1920s-30s and a Jewish population of 5,869 (59.3 percent) in 1897. Following the June 1941 German arrival, a ghetto held between 15,000 and 19,000 Jews by differing sources; on September 1, 1942, 15,000 Jews were shot, with the ghetto finally liquidated on December 13, 1943. This cemetery, likely founded in the 17th century, saw its old section badly damaged during WWII, when tombstones paved streets, before final demolition in the 1960s; the ohel of Shlomo Karliner was rebuilt in 1999.
